paper: Brandt (1977) Multi-Level Adaptive Solutions to Boundary-Value Problems, Math. Comp. 31(138), 333-390
scope_not_covered: C5 infinity-order via adaptive local refinement (MLAT)

open_questions.q: Does our from-scratch V-cycle recover Brandt's Appendix B measured factor mu ~= 0.686 when we exactly match Brandt's Cycle C configuration (trivial injection restriction, bilinear prolongation, V(1,0) GS-Lex sweep count, p^{-1}-scaled stopping) on the same 33^2 Poisson problem?
open_questions.basis: REPORT.md sec 3.1 shows our rho in [0.049, 0.061] is ~10x faster than Brandt's 0.686, and REPORT.md attributes this to our use of V(2,1) + full-weighting (which Brandt sec A.4 predicts to be faster than injection + V(1,0) Cycle C). The matching-configuration numerical check that would close the loop by directly reproducing 0.686 was not run.
open_questions.next_steps: In work/multigrid.py add a --brandt-cycle-c flag: (a) swap full-weighting for trivial injection restriction, (b) V(1,0) with lex GS instead of red-black V(2,1), (c) rerun C1 on the 33^2 Appendix B problem, (d) measure rho and check it lands in [0.6, 0.75]. Store as report/evidence/results_cyclec.json, add a row to the C1 table in REPORT.md.

open_questions.q: Is Brandt's mode-by-mode Fourier smoothing-factor prediction (mu_s = 1/2 for the 5-point Laplacian with GS-Lex, per Brandt Table 1 / sec A) numerically confirmed by our smoother alone, independent of the full V-cycle?
open_questions.basis: REPORT.md sec 2.2 substitutes red-black GS for GS-Lex on the argument that asymptotic smoothing factors match; sec 3.1 measures V-cycle rho but never isolates the smoother's error-reduction on high-frequency modes vs low-frequency modes. Brandt's local mode analysis (the theoretical prediction of the paper's Table 1) is therefore treated as an assumption, not as a directly tested claim.
open_questions.next_steps: Add work/smoothing_analysis.py: initialise a smooth-plus-oscillatory random error on the finest grid; run N smoother sweeps only (no coarse correction); FFT the error each sweep; measure per-sweep reduction factor separately in high-frequency (upper half of spectrum) and low-frequency bands. Confirm high-frequency reduction ~ 0.5/sweep and low-frequency reduction ~ 1.0/sweep, matching Brandt's smoothing-factor definition.

open_questions.q: Does Brandt's claimed insensitivity to domain shape (C4) hold when we rerun the V-cycle on a non-rectangular domain (e.g. L-shape or slit) where re-entrant corners generate singularities that dominate the fine-grid truncation error?
open_questions.basis: REPORT.md sec 1 table lists C4 as 'Partly' tested (rhs and h covered via C1; domain shape not tested). REPORT.md sec 5 explicitly labels C4 as partial. Re-entrant-corner problems are the standard stress test for whether Brandt's grid-independent factor survives when the continuum solution loses regularity.
open_questions.next_steps: Extend work/multigrid.py to mask out cells in an L-shape (remove upper-right quadrant of the unit square). Handle irregular boundary by first-order neighbour-averaging on masked-adjacent cells (Shortley-Weller if we want to preserve O(h^2)). Run C1 on the L-shape at N in {33, 65, 129, 257}. Report per-cycle rho and cycle count vs the rectangle. If rho degrades > 2x or cycle count grows with N, that is an interesting negative result on C4.

open_questions.q: Does the V(2,1) cycle count of 5 to reach 10^{-6} residual reduction remain flat if we deliberately worsen the initial guess (zero vs Brandt's 'get a good first approximation from FMG') or tighten the target reduction to 10^{-10}?
open_questions.basis: REPORT.md sec 3.2 shows exactly 5 cycles on every grid to 10^{-6}, and sec 3.1 shows exactly 8 cycles on every grid to 10^{-10}. Both counts are flat in N -- confirming O(N). But the initial-guess choice (implicitly zero) and Brandt's own recommendation of Full Multi-Grid (FMG) starting from the coarsest solution were never compared. Brandt sec 7 argues FMG gives one-cycle-to-truncation-error, which our current data cannot corroborate.
open_questions.next_steps: Add an FMG driver to work/multigrid.py: solve the coarsest 3x3 directly, prolong to next level, do one V(2,1), prolong, repeat up to the target grid. Compare vs plain V(2,1)-from-zero on cycle count to reach truncation error (~ 10^{-3} for N=33 down to ~ 4e-6 for N=513, per C3 table). If FMG achieves truncation-error accuracy in ~1 V-cycle per level as Brandt claims, that is a stronger validation of the O(N) claim than our current 5-cycles-flat table.

open_questions.q: Does Brandt's convergence factor prediction survive a switch to an anisotropic operator (e.g. epsilon * u_xx + u_yy with epsilon = 0.01), where GS-Lex is known to smooth badly in one direction?
open_questions.basis: REPORT.md sec 1 and 3 restrict all runs to the isotropic 5-point Laplacian. Brandt sec 3.3 and later work (Brandt-Livne, textbook multigrid literature) identifies anisotropy as the classic failure mode for point-wise smoothers, where grid-independent factor breaks down and semi-coarsening or line smoothers are required to recover it. This is squarely inside what Brandt's framework claims to handle qualitatively but which our tested numerical pipeline is silent on.
open_questions.next_steps: Extend work/multigrid.py operator to a*u_xx + u_yy with configurable a in {1, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001}. Rerun C1 with V(2,1) + red-black GS; expect rho to degrade toward 1.0 as a -> 0. Optionally add a line-Jacobi or line-GS smoother in the strong-coupling direction and show rho recovers. Report as a bounded generalisation of C1: 'grid-independence holds for the isotropic 5-pt Laplacian; for anisotropic operators, point smoothers are insufficient, matching Brandt sec 3.3 discussion'.
